summary: 75-ft Aermotor built 1928 at Bright Angel Point, moved 1933 to North Rim Lookout; now inactive; NHLR-registered 2009; NPS-administered per register.

facts.status_note: Inactive; no longer used for fire detection

events.note: 75-ft Aermotor tower with 7x7 cab built on Bright Angel Point
Moved from Bright Angel Point to become North Rim Lookout
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register on April 25, 2009
Listing recognized at a ceremony on July 4, 2009, held with the grand opening of the North Rim Wildland Fire and Emergency Services Facility

evidence.supports: 75-ft Aermotor tower with a 7x7 cab built in 1928 on Bright Angel Point
evidence.quote: This 75' Aermotor tower with a 7'x7' cab was built in 1928 on Bright Angel Point.

evidence.supports: Moved to become North Rim Lookout in 1933
evidence.quote: It was moved to become North Rim Lookout in 1933.

evidence.supports: Tower no longer used for fire detection
evidence.quote: The tower is no longer used for fire detection.

evidence.supports: Administered by the National Park Service
Location in Grand Canyon National Park, Coconino County
Forest Service wooden platform on Bright Angel Point before the park was established in 1919
evidence.quote: on Bright Angel Point on the North Rim prior to the establishment of Grand Canyon National Park in 1919

evidence.supports: Park Service replaced wooden platforms with steel frame towers at Bright Angel Point and Hopi Point
evidence.quote: replacing the wooden platforms with steel frame towers at Bright Angel Point and Hopi Point

evidence.supports: Park managers concerned with fires from the 1920s through the 1960s
evidence.quote: Early park managers were extremely concerned about locating and extinguishing fires

evidence.supports: Four Grand Canyon towers on the register; two on the North Rim
evidence.quote: Four historic fire lookout towers in Grand Canyon National Park, two on the North Rim and two on the South Rim, have been listed on the National Historic Lookout Register.
All four of these towers are inactive

evidence.supports: Ceremony in recognition of the lookout towers' listing, held July 4, 2009 with the grand opening of the North Rim facility
evidence.quote: was held in conjunction with the Grand Opening of the North Rim Wildland Fire and Emergency Services Facility on July 4, 2009

evidence.supports: Tower built in 1928 at Bright Angel Point and relocated in 1933; now at the summit
evidence.quote: originally constructed at Bright Angel Point and relocated here in 1933
The road to the summit is totally unpaved
A 4x4 vehicle with high clearance is required
the road is not plowed in winters

evidence.supports: Travel guide places the lookout within Kaibab National Forest
Travel guide says Edward Abbey was a seasonal lookout here in the late 1960s and 1970s
evidence.quote: served as a seasonal fire lookout post for the iconic author and environmentalist Edward Abbey during the late 1960s and 1970s

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The travel guide places the tower within Kaibab National Forest, while the register and the National Park Service place it in Grand Canyon National Park under the NPS. The register and NPS reading is used.

sources.title: Four Grand Canyon National Park Lookout Towers have been listed on the National Historic Lookout Register
How to drive the unpaved road to North Rim Lookout in Arizona

notes_for_editor: Height 22.9 m is converted from the register's 75 ft; the brief had no height. Elevation in the brief (2793.5 m) matches the register's 9,165 ft; Dangerous Roads gives 9,179 ft (2,798 m) and was not used. The April 25, 2009 registration date and the July 4, 2009 ceremony are both recorded; they are not in conflict. Staffing is not stated in the fetched pages. Public access status is not confirmed; the only road detail comes from a travel guide. The Abbey claim rests on the travel guide alone. The Forest Lookouts North Rim page gave no tower detail in the text fetched. The 'summit' location comes from the travel guide only.
